1:
Korah's descent is set out at length because it is the key to his grievance. Gill makes him a great-grandson of Levi and own cousin to Moses and Aaron — Amram the father of Moses and Izhar the father of Korah being brothers, both sons of Kohath, Amram the eldest and Izhar the next. Wesley draws the inference the Jewish writers had drawn before him: Elizaphan, whom Moses had made ruler of the Kohathites, was the son of Uzziel, the fourth son of Kohath, while Izhar stood second. A man passed over in favour of his junior's line had a standing complaint, and it broke out at last into sedition. Ellicott adds the priestly half of the same jealousy — that as the descendant of Amram's brother, Korah may well have envied the prerogatives of the priestly family itself.

The Reubenite motive was different and older. Ellicott traces Dathan and Abiram to Eliab, son of Pallu, son of Reuben, Jacob's eldest, and reads their discontent as that of a tribe which had lost the birthright and with it a leadership now held by Judah — and possibly, in their own view, a priesthood that should have descended to the firstborn. Wesley says the same, and notes what made the alliance practical: both families camped on the south side of the tabernacle. Henry turns that geography into a proverb — woe to the wicked man, and woe to his neighbour, who is in danger of being infected by him.

Whether Korah took men at all is a grammatical question, and Clarke presses it hard. The word rendered men is not in the original, and the verb is singular, so it cannot describe the act of several chiefs; every later mention of the rebellion lays it at Korah's door, and the verse should read that Korah took Dathan and Abiram and On, and they rose up. Calvin canvasses the same options — that Korah drew others in, or that he instigated himself — and settles for "he set to work." On the closing phrase of the second verse he diverges from everyone: since the word there can mean an appointed time as well as an assembly, he suspects the princes were present because they had been summoned by agreement, at a fixed hour.

Keil and Delitzsch mark what the episode is, structurally: the one important occurrence recorded from the thirty-seven years of wandering, with neither its time nor its place given, and no firm ground even for the conjecture that it fell early in that period. Ellicott offers two considerations for placing it at Kadesh — the history between the two encampments there is treated as a blank, and the narrative assumes a people concentrated in one place rather than dispersed over the face of the wilderness. On is named here and never again, and neither Henry nor Ellicott will settle the silence: he may have drawn back, or simply never made himself as conspicuous as the other two.

Calvin counts the leaders and refuses to believe the two hundred and fifty were merely swept along. Nobody eagerly embarks on so grave and invidious a contest for the sake of four men; each of them expected some prize as the reward of victory, and covered the expectation with an honourable pretext, since ambition is crafty and never destitute of a specious excuse. Ellicott, noting that Zelophehad the Manassite is expressly said not to have taken part, concludes that these princes were drawn from tribes beyond Levi.
3:
The complaint is two words in Hebrew, and they are taken in slightly different directions. Clarke gives the bare sense — too much for you — and paraphrases the spirit of it: holy offices are not equally distributed, you arrogate the most important to yourselves as if your superior holiness entitled you to them alone, whereas all the congregation are holy and have an equal right to be employed in the holiest service. Ellicott allows two readings, that Moses and Aaron have held the priesthood and the government long enough, or that it should be enough for them to be numbered among a holy people without usurping dominion over them. What Korah was actually claiming, Ellicott judges from the whole tenour of the address, was a universal priesthood on the people's behalf — with, probably, the chief place in it secured for himself.

Calvin hears something sharper than a demand for a share. The charge is one of sacrilege: Moses and Aaron have not merely usurped more than their right but robbed God of his supreme authority, impiously subjecting his inheritance to themselves. He then makes the observation that gives the verse its bite. Moses was an extraordinary example not only of integrity but of humility and gentleness, and he is here called proud and violent, as if he unworthily oppressed the people of God. God permits his servants to be loaded with such calumnies to teach them that their reward must be looked for elsewhere than from the world, and to make trial of their endurance.

The argument itself Calvin thinks self-refuting. Holiness is not destructive of subordination; it does not introduce confusion, nor release believers from the obligation to obey the laws. To infer that those whom God has sanctified are therefore not subject to the yoke is madness — and to stigmatise as tyranny the care of the people which God entrusted to his servants is to turn light into darkness on purpose.

Wesley reads the sentence clause by clause and finds the flattery in it. The people are a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exodus 19:6), therefore no less fit to offer sacrifice and incense than Aaron is; the Lord is among them by the tabernacle and the cloud, therefore ready to receive sacrifice from their own hands. He also splits the accusation in two: Moses is charged with prescribing what laws he pleases about the priesthood and confining it to his brother, Aaron with usurping it as his peculiar privilege. Whatever they intended, Wesley thinks they did not now strike directly at Moses' civil government, but at his hand in the disposal of the priesthood.

Keil and Delitzsch stop over a distinction the verse makes without comment. Two words for the congregation stand in it — one for the body as naturally organised, the other for the body as divinely summoned to a purpose — and the fact that both occur in the same sentence, they observe, is fatal to a theory built on separating them.
4:
Moses answers nothing at first. Keil and Delitzsch take his falling on his face as what it was the last time the camp turned on him — a complaint carried to the Lord rather than a gesture towards the rebels. Calvin builds his whole comment on that. Unbelievers also labour in defence of a good cause, voluntarily expose themselves to the hatred of many, and encounter great perils; but with them obstinacy stands in the place of virtue. Those who look to God know that the prosperous and unhappy events of all things are in his power, and so implore his faithfulness when adversity comes. Moses cast himself upon the earth, and that supplication was of more value than all the heroic virtues in which unbelievers have ever seemed to excel. Wesley puts the petition in five words — that God would direct and vindicate him — and Gill has him rise from the ground and speak only once the answer had come.

The trial is by incense, and the reason for that instrument is not far to seek. Keil and Delitzsch call it the holiest function of the priestly service, the one bringing a priest into the immediate presence of God; and the congregation had already been shown, in a penal judgment, how God sanctifies himself upon men who take that office without a divine call. Ellicott makes the same point at the moment the censers are ordered: the destruction of Nadab and Abihu ought to have served Korah's company as warning enough (Leviticus 10:1-3).

Why it waits until morning draws three answers. Wesley notes that morning was the hour appointed among men for administering justice, and that the delay gave the company time both to prepare their censers and to think better of the whole business. Calvin presses the mercy in it: Moses saw them carried headlong by a blind fury which could not be recalled in a moment, and granted a night in which they might be led to consideration — or, he adds, meant simply to let the tumult subside, so that all would attend to God's decision. Ellicott lets the suspension bear fruit, suggesting that On, and the sons of Korah, may have profited by it.

Keil and Delitzsch gloss the terms of the test. To be the Lord's and to be chosen by him are one thing, and the man so chosen is the one qualified to draw near, to appear before him in the sanctuary and to present the nation's sacrifices there. Clarke hears the phrase again in Paul's hands — the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, the Lord knoweth them that are his (2 Timothy 2:19) — which he calls a literal rendering of the Hebrew here, meaning that the Lord will own what is of his own appointment; and the exhortation that follows it, to depart from iniquity, alludes to the command Moses will shortly give about the tents of these wicked men.

Then the accusation is handed back. Ellicott and Clarke both mark that the closing words of the seventh verse are Korah's own, returned to him with the address altered — ye sons of Levi. Clarke reads the retort as a verdict rather than a rebuke: by their present spirit and disposition they prove themselves wholly unworthy of any spiritual employment at all.
8:
The address narrows to the tribe. Calvin explains why a speech aimed at the whole body is said to be spoken to Korah alone — he had corrupted the other Levites, and is therefore summoned first to God's tribunal, the rest included with him; and Moses could get them together quickly, since their quarters lay close to the sanctuary. The charge Calvin finds in it is ingratitude. They were not satisfied with the honour God had already given them, which betrays how little they valued his grace: had they rightly prized his gifts, each would have quietly contented himself with his lot. The more liberally a man has been dealt with, the more intolerable is his aspiring higher. And the pattern is close to universal — as soon as a person attains some middle position he raises the standard of pride and sets himself no limit until he has reached above the clouds.

Henry works from the other side, listing what the Levites already had. They were separated from the congregation of Israel, which is to say distinguished from it, so that instead of resenting Aaron's family being advanced above theirs they might have been thankful their tribe was advanced above the other tribes. It will help to keep us from envying those above us, he says, duly to consider how many there are below us. The privileges he counts as three: to draw near to God, nearer than a people already near him; to do the service of the tabernacle, since it is honour enough to bear the vessels of the sanctuary; and to stand before the congregation and minister to it — for those are truly great who serve the public, and God's service is not only perfect freedom but high preferment. Wesley says as much in a line: they were servants both of God and of the church, a high dignity, though not sufficient for ambitious minds. Gill fills in what the nearness meant in practice — a place in the courts, a watch in the house, attendance on the priests, and an ample provision by tithes.

Henry's verdict on the question itself is that undervaluing an allowed honour is what makes a man grasp at a forbidden one; those who aspire after honours forbidden them put a great contempt on the honours they have. Ellicott adds that the Targums take what Korah wanted to be the high priesthood specifically — the Levites of his company sought the priesthood, and their leader aimed at the office above it.

The last verse of the group renames the whole business, and Calvin will not let the renaming be softened. They had neither scruple nor shame in pretending pious zeal, and one word scatters the mist: they are in arms against God. Whatever they told themselves about contending with men for pre-eminence, they set out to overthrow an order God established, and he who assails God's servants assails him. Gill states the principle plainly — to resist an ordinance of God's erecting is to be gathered against God. Then comes the question Calvin thinks decides the case, and what is Aaron? Aaron has nothing of his own and arrogated nothing; the office is no idle dignity but a laborious burden laid on his shoulders for the common welfare of the church. From which Calvin turns on the Pope for likening every enemy of his tyranny to Korah, Dathan and Abiram: let such a man first produce the credentials of his calling and thoroughly fulfil his office, or he is an actor on a stage rather than a priest in a temple.
12:
The summons was to a court. Gill has Moses send messengers to bring the Reubenites to the house of judgment, where the Jewish tradition seats him with the seventy elders; Wesley notes that going up is the scriptural idiom for appearing before a place of judgment, which makes the refusal a refusal to be tried. Henry weighs the two possible reasons for it. Either they could not for shame say to his face what they were resolved to say, which would leave them some remains of modesty, or they would not own his authority at all, which is impudence of the highest degree. They spoke, he adds, the language of Pharaoh, who also set Moses at defiance — and forgot how dearly Pharaoh paid for it.

Their answer sends back four charges, and Henry takes them in order. That Moses did them an injury in bringing them out of Egypt, where they had plenty of onions and garlick and fish, but which never pretended to milk and honey; the phrase is borrowed only to mock the promise of Canaan. Gill and Ellicott both mark the perversity of the transfer, the description belonging to the land of promise alone. Calvin sees a deliberate suppression in it: they will not name Egypt while they magnify its fruitfulness, and they slide across to it the very words Moses had used, so that God's blessing may be as it were buried.

The second charge is that he meant to kill them in the wilderness, the third that he meant to enslave them by making himself a prince over them. Henry's answer to the third is biographical — Moses would gladly have declined the office at the first, and gladly resigned it many a time since, and is here given the character of a tyrant and a usurper. The fourth is that he promised a land and did not deliver it, when he had brought them to its borders and it was they who shut the door against themselves. When the foolishness of man perverteth his way, his heart fretteth against the Lord (Proverbs 19:3). As for putting out the eyes of these men, the design of everything he had done for them was to open their eyes; Ellicott notes that the same expression is used literally of Samson (Judges 16:21), and may mean here an alleged attempt to blind the people to promises broken.

Gill renders what follows as heat rather than temper — the words heated Moses exceedingly — and locates the cause not in the insult to him but in the dishonour done to God. Calvin agrees, and notices what the anger does not do: it breaks out in no reviling, as men carried away by excess assail with the tongue those who injure them. Moses betakes himself to God instead, and asks no more than that the offering be refused — all the quarrel required, since the whole matter was to be decided by God's acceptance or rejection of that incense. Clarke observes that there was never any danger of its being accepted, for God cannot bless a scheme of salvation of man's own appointment. Henry hears an older refusal underneath the words, the one recorded of Cain (Genesis 4:5) — and the epistle of Jude sets the way of Cain and the gainsaying of Korah side by side (Jude 11).

The defence itself is two clauses, and its smallness is the point. Not one ass taken, Henry says — not by way of extortion, and not by way of pay either, for he never took a general's wages or a judge's salary, and was better off keeping Jethro's flock than as king in Jeshurun. Calvin calls it the extreme of disinterestedness that a people who owed him everything had not given him the value of a single ass for all his labours.
16:
The challenge is repeated in nearly the same words, and Calvin denies that it is an experiment. Moses was not testing a doubtful matter; assured by the Spirit of prophecy what the outcome would be, he summons Korah before the tribunal of God to receive the sentence he has earned. Yet the summons is not a trap. The sacred incense-offering was itself calculated to inspire alarm — a man might still think better of attempting more than was lawful, with so memorable an example as Nadab and Abihu behind him — and Moses, relying on the command he had received, engages openly so that the judgment of God might be the more conspicuous.

Wesley settles the staging. The trial could not be held inside the tabernacle: the place set apart for incense was too small for so many men offering severally, and none but priests might enter it at all. So they stood at the door, by Moses' direction and for this occasion only — where the people, who were to be instructed by the experiment, could see the proof of it. The censers themselves are a small puzzle. Gill takes them for vessels the heads of families had used before the office was confined to Aaron's house, or else a sort of chafing dish that would serve the present purpose; Ellicott allows both and adds a third, that Korah's company may simply have made them. On the fire the witnesses are definite: it came from the altar of burnt offering, strange fire being what had killed Nadab and Abihu, and Wesley thinks the memory of that death was precisely what kept them to the altar.

What Calvin cannot get past is that they came at all. If any spark of the fear of God had remained in them the censers would have fallen straight out of their hands; Korah appears rather to have sought out how he might cast aside all fear and bereave himself of his senses. The gathering of the congregation is read the same way — an ostentatious hardening, in which he collects a crowd so that the magnificence of his array might overwhelm the grace of God which opposed him, as though a man could put out the light of the sun by interposing a little smoke. Ambitious men do collect their forces by ingratiating themselves with others, and if the world approves them they grow drunk on that confidence.

How the crowd was got is Gill's contribution, out of Jarchi: Korah spent the night going from tribe to tribe, protesting that he acted not for his own private interest but for the public good, against two men who had taken to themselves the one the kingdom and the other the priesthood. It worked. Ellicott and Wesley both find in the wording a general disposition in the people to favour the insurrection, and Wesley suspects they assembled to be witnesses of a success they did not doubt, and to fall upon Moses and Aaron when it came. Calvin marks the same thing as levity — they had been long accustomed to a priesthood they knew God had instituted, and a single night was enough to turn them.

Then the cloud brightened. Wesley describes the glory as appearing in it with greater brightness and majesty than usual, a token of God's approach; Henry sets the appearance beside the one that installed Aaron at the first (Leviticus 9:23) and reads this second one as confirming him in the office and confounding those who had set up against him. Nothing, Henry adds, is more terrible to men conscious of guilt than the appearance of the divine glory.
20:
The sentence falls on the whole assembly rather than on the ringleaders, and the reason is given carefully. Gill points out that the order names this congregation, not Korah's two hundred and fifty — the people who had come at his call and stood with him had shown by that association whose side they were on. Ellicott says it flatly: by obeying Korah's summons the congregation, or a large part of it, had made themselves partakers in his sin. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a legal fact — assembling in front of the tabernacle was making common cause with the rebels, and it is that which is threatened with sudden destruction.

Calvin reads the command to separate as a mercy shown to the two men addressed. God had drawn Lot out of Sodom by the hand of an angel before destroying it, and here he asks room to exercise his wrath, as if he were not free to execute vengeance until his servants were out of the way. But he is careful about what such a sentence is. It does not publish what God has determined in his secret counsel; it pronounces what the authors of the wickedness have deserved, God ascending his judgment-seat. The intercession that follows therefore changed no eternal decree — it delivered the people from a punishment they had merited. When scripture says God is influenced by prayer, he adds, it does not mean that he takes on new feelings after the manner of men, but that out of a more than paternal love he indulges us by listening to our desires.

Nor did the threat forbid the prayer; Calvin thinks it was designed to quicken Moses' earnestness, since necessity inflames the zeal of the godly, and his conviction that the covenant made with Abraham could not be voided was engraved deeply enough to surmount whatever seemed to contradict it.

The address itself is what every witness stops over. Clarke takes it as evidence about the soul: to call God the God of the spirits of all flesh proves that these men held man to be compounded of flesh and spirit, and the two principles perfectly distinct. He will not allow the usual escape that the word means only breath — the phrase would then run, absurdly, the God of the breaths of all flesh — and he sets the same construction beside its parallels (Job 12:10). Calvin draws a further inference from the same words: God is not said here to have inspired all flesh with life but to have created their spirits, so that each man has his own — which he turns against the Manichean notion that souls are so derived from the Spirit of God that there is finally only one spirit.

The plea underneath the title is the potter's. Calvin has Moses urging God to preserve his own work as a potter spares the vessels he has formed, and compares Isaiah's prayer that we are the clay and he our potter (Isaiah 64:8) — noting that Isaiah appeals to the special grace given to a people, while Moses reaches further back, to the general grace of creation. Wesley unfolds the title into four pleas at once: maker of spirits, destroy not thy own workmanship; preserver and Lord of them; father of them, deal mercifully with thy own children; and searcher of them, who can distinguish those who maliciously raised the tumult from those whose simple credulity made them a prey to crafty seducers. Henry hears Abraham at Sodom in the question that closes the prayer (Genesis 18:23), and grants what Wesley's last plea implies — that joining in was the sin of them all, but the great transgression belonged to the man who first hatched the treason.
23:
Where the rebels were is worth establishing, and Henry establishes it. Dathan and Abiram had set up a spacious tent in the middle of their families' quarters, where they kept court and met in council and hung out their flag of defiance; there they stayed while Korah went up to the sanctuary door, waiting to hear how the trial went. They never heard. Their business was finished before that trial was over, God taking what method he pleases in his judgments. Ellicott is less sure what the word for their dwelling means: it usually denotes the boarded structure the tent-covering was laid over, which raises the possibility of a rival tabernacle, but he prefers a collective reading — Korah's tent pitched defiantly near the Reubenites, with the tents of Dathan and Abiram — because the command as Moses delivers it says tents.

Henry hears in the order an answer to the prayer just offered, and draws a hard corollary from it. The congregation will not be destroyed, provided they shift for their own safety; and the man who prayed for them must now go and preach to them, because we cannot reap the benefit of our friends' prayers unless we ourselves are diligent in using the means of salvation. God never promised to save by miracle those who would not save themselves by means. Calvin puts the condition the other way round: in commanding them to withdraw, God implies that whoever stays mixed up with the rebels will share the destruction.

Moses goes down to the men who would not come up to him. Ministers must with meekness instruct those who oppose themselves, Henry says, and not think it beneath them to stoop to the most stubborn for their good — Christ himself stretches out his hand to a gainsaying people. The elders go with him for his protection against the insolence of the crowd and to put an honour on him; Wesley adds that their presence gave the act greater solemnity. Calvin notes that these elders had plainly held to Moses' side, which is a reason for not reading the condemnation of the congregation without exception: Caleb and Joshua were never drawn into such a sin.

The command to depart is sharp, and Calvin defends its sharpness. Moses does not name the three but calls them these wicked men, which is not the reviling of anger but an urgent mode of exhortation — had he not marked his detestation so vehemently, his words might have been coldly received. The warning against being consumed in their sins is of the same kind, and means, lest the contagion of so many and such great crimes infect you. Henry reads the withdrawal as a public act, by which the people disowned the rebels' cause and dreaded the punishment coming; those who would not perish with sinners must come out from among them and be separate (Revelation 18:4).

They obeyed, which Calvin takes as evidence that most of them had been carried away by folly rather than malice, since deliberate iniquity is not corrected so easily. The two Reubenites did not. Henry has them standing in their tent doors as if they would outface God himself, and pities the little children put by their parents' presumption into so audacious a posture; Wesley reads the posture as a declaration that they feared neither God nor man. Calvin doubts they were unafraid — stripped of all aid and favour they must have been terrified — but says they stood like maniacs, as the wicked often stand, astounded and yet never thinking to appease God. Ellicott observes what the verse leaves out: Korah's own position is not given, nor are his sons here, who did not die (Numbers 26:11), and whose family produced Samuel the prophet, Heman the singer, and the name that stands in the titles of eleven psalms.
28:
What exactly was on trial is spelled out by the phrase all these works, and the witnesses fill it in from the history. Gill lists the bringing of Israel out of Egypt, the exchange of the firstborn for the Levites, the consecration of Aaron and his sons, the gift of the Levites to the priests, and the setting of Elizaphan over the Kohathites — every one of them a thing these men had found fault with. Wesley's list runs the same way and adds the conducting of the people through the wilderness and the giving of laws about the priesthood; Ellicott's ends with the general commission to declare the Lord's will to the people. The disclaimer attached to it is the whole point of the appeal: not one of these was done out of Moses' own mind.

Calvin sees why the contest had to be brought to this pitch. The object was that God should sanction before the whole nation, by a terrible exertion of his power, the system he had himself established — and it was no ordinary confidence that conceded the victory to his enemies unless the earth should swallow them alive. Moses could fairly have claimed vindication if the men had been cut off by any sudden stroke. Instead he offers to be accounted an impostor if they die as men commonly die.

The two halves of the wager are drawn precisely. Gill takes the common death to mean what carries off most men, a fever or the wearing out of old age; Wesley separates that from the second clause, which he reads as any of the usual judgments — plague, or the sword — and puts the offer in the plainest words anyone gives it: I am content that you take me for an impostor, falsely pretending to be sent of God. Henry runs the same list and adds fire from heaven to it, since fire from heaven had precedent and this appeal required something with none.

Everything therefore turns on the word for what the Lord is asked to do. Clarke and Ellicott both render it literally — if the Lord create a creation — and take it to mean an act hitherto unknown. Calvin says the same and presses the force of the term: the manner of their death would be as unusual as if God were to add something to his creation and change the face of the world. He hears the memory of it in the psalm that prays for the wicked to go down alive into the grave, memorable punishments passing into proverbial instances of God's wrath (Psalms 55:23).

Clarke uses the other key word to settle a question of translation, and his argument is from what the sentence includes. The pit swallows their households and their goods along with them; it would be absurd to suppose that a man's house had gone to hell, and worse than absurd to imagine his little children there, so the word must here mean a chasm in the earth and not the place of the lost.

Henry adds what the prediction does that the judgment alone would not. An unprecedented death would have proved God's displeasure with the rebels in any case; foretold beforehand, with no natural indication of it whatever, it proved something further about the man who foretold it — that he was intimately acquainted with the divine counsels, and could obtain such appearances of divine power in his own vindication. And it answered the calculation that had made Dathan and Abiram feel safe so far from the tabernacle, on the old principle that whoever is far from Jove is far from the thunderbolt. The earth would serve God's justice as effectually as the fire.
31:
Gill dates the event to the syllable — as soon as the speech was finished, and, on Josephus' account, after a long prayer which that writer sets out at length. Keil and Delitzsch describe what followed as a closing as well as an opening: the ground clave, took them with their families and their possessions, and shut above them, so that they perished without a trace from among the congregation. The households in question, they add, are people and not tents. Gill lets the verb do the work the Hebrew gives it, the earth opening its mouth as a beast of prey opens its mouth, and taking them as such a creature takes its prey.

Whether Korah went down with them is the one substantial dispute in the chapter, and the case against it is built from other passages. Ellicott concedes that this verse alone would suggest he did, and that a later summary names him with Dathan and Abiram; but his sons did not die (Numbers 26:11), Deuteronomy speaks only of what was done to Dathan and Abiram and their households, and the psalm that rehearses the story divides the two punishments cleanly, the earth swallowing the one pair and the flame burning up the wicked (Psalms 106:17-18). He thinks it most natural that Korah stood at the tabernacle door with his two hundred and fifty and shared their death, and cites Ibn Ezra's parallel: the song at the Red Sea names only the chariots and the host, while a psalm names Pharaoh himself among the overthrown. Wesley reaches the same conclusion by an argument about command — a captain does not desert his men and leave them without a head, least of all with Aaron, his great adversary, still standing there — and supposes the sons who lived to have been absent on some service of the tabernacle, God so ordering it by providence.

Clarke sums the arithmetic of the judgment in a line: two distinct punishments, the pit and the fire, for the two divisions of these rebels. Calvin thinks the division deliberate. A diversity of punishments awakened more astonishment than one death for all would have done, and made plain that each received a recompense according to the measure of his iniquity. Of the fire he says only that it went out from Jehovah because it was not kindled naturally or by accident but came with marks that showed who sent it; Gill takes it for flashes of lightning out of the cloud.

Gill describes the cry as so piercing that the Israelites fled to get out of the sound of it as much as for their own safety, and the Targum supplies the words the dying were held to have cried: that the Lord is righteous and his judgments truth, and true the words of Moses his servant, and we wicked who have rebelled against him. Calvin watches the flight rather than the cry. The people were standing at a distance, having already withdrawn in token of separation, and their bolting is the mark of a bad conscience, which is always troubled in itself. The godly too ought to be alarmed by God's judgments, so that their dread may school them in his fear; but hypocrites fall down as though the lightning had struck their own heads — and that blind fear, as the next day showed, profited them little.

Henry keeps in view one detail that is easy to lose: Aaron was standing among the men the fire consumed, and was preserved alive. Had they been content with the office of Levites they might have lived and died with joy and reputation; aiming at honours not appointed them, like the angels who left their first estate, they had their censers struck out of their hands and their breath out of their bodies.
36:
The censers survive their owners, and the instruction is precise. Keil and Delitzsch render the order as taking them up from between the burning — from the midst of the men who had been burned — and scattering the coals far off so the fire could not be used again. The vessels had become holy by being brought before the Lord, so that when the men who brought them were killed the censers fell to him as banned things (Leviticus 27:28). Clarke glosses the word as consecrated to God's service, improperly employed.

Why Eleazar and not Aaron is answered the same way three times over. Aaron was about to be needed for an act of priestly intercession, Ellicott says, and contact with the dead would have disqualified him; Gill adds that giving the task to the man who would succeed to the high priesthood confirmed the office in Aaron's line. Wesley thinks the rough part of the work simply more proper for the younger man, and pictures what he had to handle — bodies left where they fell, the fire having taken their lives as lightning sometimes does without consuming them. The coals went yonder: far from the sanctuary, in the unclean place where the ashes were cast, so that God's rejection of their service was visible in the disposal of it. Henry reads that act as a verdict on the offering, a polluted thing scattered outside the camp, since the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination.

What is done with the metal turns the judgment into furniture. Henry notes that they were not kept as censers, which would have put honour on the usurpers, and that the golden altar had golden ones already; they were beaten flat and laid over the brazen altar instead — so that the vessels which had challenged Aaron's office ended by adorning and protecting the altar where he ministered. Ellicott explains what the addition was worth: the altar was wood under brass, and a second layer gave further security against a fire that burned on it continually.

Calvin puts a different construction on the holiness that saved them from the scrap heap. Some take it that things once devoted to God's service could not be turned to profane uses; he thinks rather that they were set apart as accursed, which is why the fire in them was flung away while the metal was kept — kept as a thing under a ban, so that every generation after might understand that none but priests were admitted to the sacrifices. Nor is it idle, he adds, that the men are called sinners against their own souls: the memory of their punishment was engraved on those plates to awaken a continuing dread.

The reason given for the whole arrangement is memory, and Calvin is blunt about why memory needed help. God's judgments, which ought to stay in full remembrance in every age, are blotted out of men's minds unless they are given aids to meditate on them — less from ignorance than from neglect. Henry says the same from the other side: impressions that seem deep are not always durable, and the record was appointed so that the Levites who served at this altar might learn to keep within their bounds. Ellicott notes that the epistle of Jude puts the same example to Christians.

One small question the witnesses answer differently. Gill takes the priests' censers to have been silver — gold for the high priest on the day of atonement, silver otherwise — and reads the specification of brass here as marking Korah's vessels off from Aaron's. Ellicott knows the opinion and rejects it, finding no sufficient authority for silver and pointing to the statement that all the vessels of the altar were brass (Exodus 38:3); gold he allows only for the censers of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 7:50).
41:
One day is all the interval. Henry sets the scene by what had not yet faded: the shrieks of the sinking men still sounding, the smell of the fire in the air, the ground scarcely closed — and the same sin re-enacted over it. Calvin adds that the plates were at that moment being beaten out precisely so the judgment should not be forgotten, and asks the two questions the charge cannot survive: was it in the power of Moses to command the earth to open, or to draw fire down from heaven at will? Clarke supplies the only answer that makes the accusation intelligible — the people must have persuaded themselves that some cunning was used, and the earthquake and the fire contrived; otherwise they could hardly have dared the anger of the Lord in the face of his justice.

The wording of the charge is what appals them. Henry says it canonises the rebels, giving the title of the people of the Lord to men who died in arms against him; and since Moses and Aaron had done what they could to save them, to charge the two with murder was in effect to charge God with it. Calvin makes the same two counts: they put Moses and Aaron in God's place as the authors of the killing, and they sanctify the corpses in his despite — reckoning among the people of God men whom he had cut off from the human race. Ellicott can conceive no more striking illustration of the depravity of the human heart; Henry draws a practical conclusion, that if neither the terrors of the law nor those of the judgments could change these men, grace must — love will do what fear could not.

The crowd closed in. Gill takes the gathering for an attempt on their lives, the Targum saying so outright. What stopped it was the cloud. Keil and Delitzsch note that it stood over the tabernacle continually while the camp was pitched, so that its covering the tent here must mean something fuller than usual — as at the first erection — with the glory breaking out of the darkness in a miraculous splendour; Ellicott suspects it had been withdrawn during the previous day's judgment and was now restored to hearten the two men.

Calvin reads the shelter as a measure of the danger. The glory stood over the tabernacle, not over the men, who remained perfectly open to stoning; what protected them was that the sight dazzled the eyes of those who meant to do it. They had fled there because in the extremity of their danger no other hope was left, and God received them under the shadow of his wings — his standing testimony that the prayers of his people are never spent for nothing, since he is near to all who cast their care upon him even where no visible dwelling marks the place. Gill notes that they did not go inside but stood at the door; in all their distresses, as Wesley puts it, they made God their refuge.

The sentence that follows is the one they heard the day before, and Keil and Delitzsch mark the difference in what came of it: they fell on their faces and prayed as before, but this time the judgment was not turned aside. Calvin takes the command to withdraw as more than a movement — they were separated already, standing at the sanctuary — and reads it as an order to sever themselves from the people altogether, casting away all care for the common welfare. What they did instead he calls an incredible kindness: forgetful of lives they could see were in danger, they set about making atonement for men who had been plotting their destruction. Wesley puts it in three words, rendering good for evil.
46:
The remedy is a censer, and Ellicott would make it the censer — the high priest's golden one — incense standing for prayer and figuring Christ's intercession (Psalms 141:2). Wesley reads the errand the same way, incense being a sign of intercession and meant to be accompanied by it. That it happened outside the sanctuary at all is extraordinary: both note that incense might ordinarily be offered only on the golden altar within, and nothing but an express command could warrant carrying it into the camp.

Clarke explains the form the plague took. It came as a secret blast, which no one could attribute to human contrivance; God's hand alone was visible in the stroke and in the manner of its arrest, and it had to be so, that the congregation might see that the men who perished were not the people of the Lord, and that God and not Moses destroyed them.

Calvin is careful that the censer not be mistaken for the cause. The expiation did not depend on an incense-offering, and God is not appeased by the savour of frankincense; a symbol was set before a gross-hearted people to rouse them to repentance and faith. It taught two things — that the priesthood they despised was the very thing in which divine power displays itself for life or for death, and that God was propitious to them only by virtue of a mediator, Aaron standing in the office until the true and perpetual one should be revealed.

What Aaron does with it Henry describes with unusual warmth. He burned the incense not to purify infected air but to pacify an offended God; and forgetting his age and his gravity he ran, refusing to let them smart a while so that his coming might be more welcome. It was courage as much as charity — into a rabble enraged against him, and into a mortality where thousands were falling on either hand. Then the comparison the chapter has been building towards: set Aaron's censer beside the censers of those sinners against their own souls, and the one provoked God's anger where the other pacified it.

Where he stood is what is remembered. Gill has the plague moving from one end of the camp onward, Aaron placing himself between the part it had wasted and the part it had not reached — the Targum picturing him at prayer, making a partition with his censer between the dead and the living. All three take the posture as a figure of the mediator between the living God and dead sinners. Ellicott points to the offering for a sweet-smelling savour (Ephesians 5:2); Clarke reasons from lesser to greater — if a high priest with a censer could disarm that wrath, how much more the atonement of which the sacrifices and the incense were the two halves of a shadow, the death purchasing and the intercession sparing (Romans 5:10). He draws the chapter's warning from the same place: God is jealous of the sole right of appointing how men are saved, or Korah's new service would not have been resented so terribly.

The toll closes the argument the murmurers began. They had cried out that the people of the Lord were slain when, as Calvin reckons them, some three hundred had died; they now learn how much better it would have been to be silent before God than to see nearly fifty times that number destroyed, obstinacy making him redouble his punishments as he had threatened (Leviticus 26:18). Paul's warning against murmuring stands on this history (1 Corinthians 10:10). Gill sees in the number one more instalment of the sentence that their carcases should fall in the wilderness, and notes that the plague had stopped before Aaron left the camp, the closing verse repeating it to show that it stayed stopped.
